newsitem.title: TURKEY: China seen having low profile on world corn market.
newsitem.headline: China seen having low profile on world corn market.

text.p: China is unlikely to be either a major importer or exporter of corn this year, a senior Cargill grains trader predicted on Tuesday.
China, facing sharp rises in domestic corn demand due to rising meat consumption, banned exports of the grain in 1994 but its future trade plans remained uncertain, he said.

"We know that there are good stocks of corn in the producing provinces of the northeast but central government has shown no signs of wanting to lift the export ban imposed in 1994," Fausto Filice, responsible for non-U.S. coarse grains trading at Cargill International in Geneva, told an industry conference.
China appeared to have a bigger corn crop this year but demand for feed grain was also likely to keep growing.
And domestic prices were now higher than world market levels, so exports would require some form of subsidy, which Filice thought unlikely.
"Anything can happen in China but for the coming year I don't see China as being either a big exporter or importer of corn," he said.
The International Grains Council sees China's corn (maize) output rising four million tonnes to 108 million this year.
It predicts China will import two million tonnes.
China's meat demand surged between 1980 and 1995 to nearly 50 million tonnes from a little over 10 million tonnes, according to figures given at the conference.
"In China meat consumption this year will be two and a half times what it was in 1986," Filice said.
Assuming projected 1997 economic growth of some eight to nine percent fed through into higher incomes, meat demand would rise even further.
Filice predicted China's current per capita annual meat consumption of 43 kilos would reach 50 kilos after the turn of the century.
Increased Asian demand for feed grain, driven mainly by meat as wealthier populations chose richer diets, was one of three big factors behind record corn prices this year, he said.
Others were competition from the oilseeds sector for arable land at the expense of grain and past European and U.S. policies designed to shield farmers from market forces.
